analysis.one_liner: Requires car companies to get your explicit consent before selling or sharing your car and location data.
analysis.headline: The Car Privacy Rights Act, introduced in September 2024 with two cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern connected cars collect where you drove, how hard you braked, and where you park — and some companies sell that data to brokers and insurers. This bill would make it illegal for carmakers, insurers, and app companies to sell or share your car data unless you first got a clear notice and said yes. You could take back your consent any time, carmakers and insurers would have to report their data practices to the Federal Trade Commission each year, and the FTC would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Every driver and passenger whose connected car tracks location, driving behavior, and vehicle status — the bill puts you, rather than the manufacturer, in charge of who gets that data.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to share or sell a person's car data — including driving history, vehicle condition, and precise location down to street level or within 1,850 feet — unless the company gave a clear, standalone notice and the consumer explicitly agreed [S2].
Bars companies from treating acceptance of a general terms-of-service agreement as consent, and requires that consent be easy to revoke through the company's website, app, or mail [S2].

Requires every car manufacturer and motor vehicle insurance company to report annually to the FTC on what car data it collects, why, and who it is sold or shared with, with the FTC summarizing the results publicly for Congress [S2].

Directs the FTC, with the FCC and the auto safety agency, to issue guidance within 180 days on how carmakers should address domestic violence risks in apps that can pinpoint a person's or vehicle's precise location [S2].
Enforces all of this under the FTC's existing authority over unfair and deceptive practices, backed by rulemaking power and penalties [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Car manufacturers, motor vehicle insurers, and app companies that currently monetize driving and location data — they would lose that revenue and bear notice, consent, and annual reporting costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill restricts sharing and selling but does not stop companies from collecting car data in the first place; a manufacturer could still gather location and driving history and simply hold it [S2].

It carves out an exception letting companies share data with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration without consumer consent, and its only enforcement path is through the FTC — an individual driver could not sue on their own [S2].
Compliance would cost manufacturers and insurers real money: standalone notices for each data category, consent-confirmation systems, revocation channels, and annual privacy reports [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — control over data that reveals where you live, work, and drive, which can feed insurance pricing, advertising, and stalking — is broad and personal, and the costs are one-time compliance burdens plus lost data revenue for the companies. The bill's real weakness is design: it leaves collection itself untouched and gives individuals no right to sue, so its protection depends entirely on FTC enforcement. As written, it is a meaningful but partial fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee on September 25, 2024, and nothing further happened — no hearing, no vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Car Privacy Rights Act of 2024 on September 25, 2024, joined by Sen. Elizabeth Warren [S1] [S2].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S4].
The bill attracted two cosponsors, both Democrats, and no member of the other party signed on [S3].
The committee never took the bill up, and the congressional record shows no action after the referral [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers, insurers, and the data brokers that buy and resell driving and location records are better off — the existing market for that data continues unchanged, and drivers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's only support was from three Democrats, and it died in a committee controlled by the majority party without opposition ever being tested.

industries.note: The bill would end a revenue stream: selling or sharing driving records, vehicle status, and precise location without asking. It would also impose notice, consent, and annual reporting duties. The industry's interest in keeping that data flowing runs directly against drivers' control over their own information.

industries.industry: Motor vehicle insurers and auto-data brokers
industries.note: Insurers are covered entities under the bill and, like manufacturers, could no longer receive or share driving data without explicit consent; they would also file annual privacy reports. Brokers that turn driving behavior into scores for insurers would lose their supply of consent-free data, which today can raise individual premiums.

Companies that gather car data through phone and in-car apps fall under the bill's consent and reporting rules. Apps that can pinpoint a vehicle or a person's location would face federal guidance on protecting domestic violence victims.
